facts.fact: The Asian arowana (Scleropages formosus) is an obligate predator that reaches up to 900 mm standard length; Seriously Fish rates it difficult to keep.
Wild Asian arowana live in blackwater rivers and slow forest swamps of Southeast Asia, and the green form occurs in Vietnam, Cambodia, Thailand, Myanmar, Malaysia and Indonesia.
The Asian arowana has been on CITES Appendix I since 1975; captive-bred fish from registered farms may be traded and should be microchipped and come with papers.
The IUCN lists the Asian arowana as Endangered.
Arowana mature late, at about 3–4 years; the female lays only 30–100 large eggs, and the male broods eggs and larvae in his mouth.
Tank: at least 2 m long; Seriously Fish says the species suits only public aquaria or the very largest home tanks.
A tight-fitting lid is essential because Asian arowana are strong jumpers.
Water for Asian arowana: 22–28 °C, pH 5.0–8.0, hardness 2–15 dGH.
Wikipedia gives 24–30 °C and well-filtered, soft, slightly acidic water for Asian arowana.
Weekly water changes of 30–50% are described as mandatory for arowana.
Arowana need high dissolved oxygen; external filters, powerheads or airstones help.
Never add an arowana to a new, biologically immature aquarium; it needs stable, well-established conditions.
Food for young arowana: bloodworm, small earthworms and chopped prawn.
Food for adult arowana: fish strips, whole prawns, mussels, live river shrimp and larger earthworms; dried pellets should not be the staple.
Do not feed mammal or bird meat (beef heart, chicken): arowana may not metabolise some of these fats, which can cause fat deposits and organ damage.
Avoid feeder fish such as livebearers or small goldfish: they can bring in parasites or disease and are often poor nutrition.
Sources disagree on feeder fish: Wikipedia lists feeder fish among typical arowana foods, alongside shrimp and crickets.
Arowana feed mainly at the water surface.
Seriously Fish rates Asian arowana as needing careful choice of tankmates and as fine kept alone.
Vietnamese keepers often house arowana with cá hổ (tigerfish/datnoid) in midwater and cá sam (bottom dweller); arowana hold the top layer and try to dominate it.
Ngân Long (silver arowana) is described as gentle and is often kept with other arowana types.
Vietnamese keepers feed arowana sâu (worms/larvae), dế (crickets), tôm (shrimp), trạch (loach) and rết (centipedes); young fish get small shrimp torn into pieces.
Keepers in Vietnam fear sudden temperature changes and abrupt water changes most; in northern winters they cover the tank and use heaters, and in summer use a stainless mesh cover.
Common arowana problems named by Vietnamese keepers are nấm (fungus) and xù vẩy (raised scales).

Vietnamese variety names: Ngân Long (silver), Kim Long (gold), Thanh Long (green/blue), Huyết Long (red), Hắc Long (black, Osteoglossum ferreirai), Kim Long Quá Bối (crossback gold), Cao Lưng Hồng Vỹ (red-tail golden).
Vietnamese dealers import arowana from Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia; fish are microchipped at 4–5 months and 12–15 cm.
Colour takes about 1–2 years to develop in Kim Long and 2–3 years in Huyết Long, depending on diet, light, water and genetics.
Vietnamese shop names for arowana diseases: bệnh kênh mang (gill curl), xù vảy (raised scales/dropsy), trướng bụng (bloat), đốm trắng (white spot/ich).
"Cháy lưng" is the Vietnamese name for darkened, dull back scales on arowana.
"Dư môi" is the Vietnamese name for an overgrown, usually lower, lip that makes an arowana's mouth uneven.
Vietnamese keepers use "rết" for centipedes fed live to cá rồng (arowana); one reported price was about 12,000–20,000 VND per centipede in Hanoi.
A keeper reports trapping cockroaches (gián) as live food for flowerhorn (cá La Hán) and arowana, using an oiled jar with leftover food as bait.
Keepers warn that cockroaches exposed to insecticide can kill a fish within hours, so only unsprayed roaches should be fed.
Drop eye (eye droop): one or both eyes turn downward as if looking at the floor; it rarely resolves on its own and can worsen.
Drop eye is seen mainly in bonytongues: Asian and silver arowana and Arapaima gigas.
Keepers report drop eye most often in silver arowana from about 16 inches, and only occasionally in large Asian arowana.
Proposed causes of drop eye include looking down for food, fat behind the eyes, poor nutrition, inbreeding, mechanical injury, stress, too much light, clear-sided tanks and mycobacteriosis.
Jay Hemdal thinks the main cause of drop eye is injury from striking the tank sides or lid, especially in clear-sided tanks.
There is no proven cure for drop eye; floating red ping-pong balls, moving fish to ponds and surgery have been tried or reported.
Floating ping-pong balls to make arowana look up is said not to work by a MonsterFishKeepers disease guide, and Jay Hemdal questions the idea.
Arowana and arapaima rarely if ever develop drop eye in ponds; avoiding clear-sided tanks may help.
Gill curl: gill covers become concave and curl outward, breathing is irregular, the fish gasps at the surface and loses appetite (keeper report).
Keepers link gill curl to fouled water (ammonia, nitrite, nitrate), too little space or nutrition while growing, and large temperature swings.
For early gill curl, keepers change about 20% of the water at once and every 2–3 days, and raise oxygen and water flow; hardened curled covers need surgery by a professional.
Raised-scale disease mostly hits young arowana: scales lift with blood at their bases, then redden and drop off (keeper report).
Keepers blame raised scales in arowana on sharp temperature changes and dirty water.
Fish lice and anchor worms on arowana usually come in with live food (keeper report).
Keepers advise quarantining live foods for a few days before feeding them to arowana.
Bloat in young arowana starts as a swollen belly with a red, swollen vent and can progress to loss of balance with the head dipping (keeper report).
Keepers attribute bloat in young arowana to stale food or injury to the stomach wall.
